title: Log a thing
description: Build a one-page app that saves what you type and lists it back — and learn the one rule that explains where every database call goes. The Visual Function computes; the canvas does the waiting; the signal wire is the await.

steps.title: What you are about to build
steps.body:
## Log a thing

A text field, a **Log it** button, and a list that fills up. Nothing you have not seen. What makes it worth twenty minutes is where the work is divided.

The page already has its furniture: the field, the button, a status line and an empty card. You are going to add the four nodes that make it do something, and a collection to put the entries in.

### The one rule

You will reach for a **Visual Function** to check what was typed. Then you will want it to save the record too — and there is no block for that, in this or any other Visual Function.

That is deliberate, and it is the whole point of this lesson:

**The Visual Function computes. The canvas does the waiting. The signal wire is the await.**

A block program runs start to finish in one go. It cannot pause halfway through for a database. So it does the thinking, and then it sends a signal — and the node on the other end of that wire does the part that takes time.

steps.title: Make somewhere to put them
steps.body:
Open the **Data** panel and create a collection called `LogEntries`, with one text column called `title`.

Spell both exactly as written — the rest of the lesson wires to those two names, and a typo here shows up three steps later as a node with no port to connect.

If this project has no database yet, the Data panel offers to make one. Say yes: it creates a database that belongs to this project and to nothing else on your machine.

steps.title: Add the Visual Function
steps.body:
Add a **Visual Function** node to the canvas and rename it to `Check the entry`.

Open it, and give it one input to work with:

- **Define input** named `entry`, type `string`

Close the block editor. The node now has an `entry` port on its left. Drag from the **Entry field**'s `Text` output into it.

That wire is the only way the typed text reaches the program. A block program cannot read the canvas; it reads its own inputs.

steps.title: Teach it to decide
steps.body:
Back inside `Check the entry`, build the program. Declare what it will produce:

- **Define output** `title`, type `string`
- **Define output** `message`, type `string`
- **Define signal output** `ok`
- **Define signal output** `bad`

Then one **if / else**, on **not** `get input entry`:

- **if** there is no entry: set output `message` to `Type something first, then press Log it.`, then **send signal** `bad`
- **else**: **set variable** `lastEntryTitle` to `get input entry`, set output `title` from **get variable** `lastEntryTitle`, set output `message` to nothing, then **send signal** `ok`

Two signal outputs from one program is the fan-out this lesson is about. Each one is a separate wire, and the canvas decides what happens on each.

Now wire the outside: the **Log it button**'s `Click` into the function's `Run`, and the function's `message` into the **Status line**'s `Text`.

steps.title: Do the saving on the canvas
steps.body:
Add a **Create Record** node, rename it `Save the entry`, and set its **Class** to `LogEntries`.

Wire two things into it:

- the function's `ok` signal into **Do**
- the function's `title` value into the **title** property port

This is the split the rule is about. The program decided; it did not save. It sent `ok`, and the wire is what makes the saving happen after the deciding.

And notice what crossed with it: `title` is a value the program worked out and had to hand over on a port, because the two halves are two nodes. That is the price of the split, and `lastEntryTitle` in the block program is the tool for paying it — a variable outlives one run of one program, so a second Visual Function after the save can still read it.

steps.title: Read them back
steps.body:
Two nodes, and the list works.

Add a **Query Records** node, rename it `Read the entries`, set its **Class** to `LogEntries`. Then add a **Repeater** inside the **Saved entries** card, rename it `One row per entry`, and set its **Template** to `/Components/LogRow` — a row component the project already carries, because a Repeater's template is always a component and never a node.

Wire three things:

- the query's `Items` into the repeater's `Items`
- the page's `Did Mount` into the query's `Do`, so the list is there when the page opens
- **Save the entry**'s `Done` into the query's `Do`, so it refreshes after each save

That last wire is worth a second look. The Visual Function's finishing signal is called **Success**; Create Record's is called **Done**. Both are on this canvas, two nodes apart, and both are right — a Visual Function reports that its program succeeded, and a record node reports that its request came back. Read the port, not the word you expected.

steps.title: Log something
steps.body:
Open the preview, type a line and press **Log it**. It should appear in the card below.

Then press **Log it** on an empty field. Nothing is saved, and the status line tells you why — that is the `bad` branch, and it never touched the database at all.

This step is not complete until there is at least one record in `LogEntries`. A graph that looks right and saves nothing is the failure this check exists to catch.

steps.title: What you just learned
steps.body:
## The rule, now that you have used it

**The Visual Function computes. The canvas does the waiting. The signal wire is the await.**

There is no `create record` block, no `fetch` block, no `navigate` block. There is a **Create Record** node, a **REST** node and a **Navigate** node — one sentence instead of five exceptions.

And the runtime makes the handoff safe: a Visual Function flags every output it wrote **before** it fires its finishing signal. So a graph sequenced on that signal reads values that are already up to date. That guarantee is what lets a wire stand in for an `await`.

### The cost, stated plainly

Splitting a program at every data call means state has to be re-threaded through ports across the split. You felt it when `title` had to cross on a wire. **Set variable** and **get variable** are how you carry a value further than one run of one program — that is what `lastEntryTitle` was for, and it is why they are in the block set.

If you ever find yourself splitting one job across **three or more** Visual Functions just to thread state, that is worth reporting. It is the one thing that would make us revisit this.
